As a reminder, the Fairfax County Economic Mobility Pilot was launched in October of 2023. The initiative provided 180 randomly selected households with monthly cash payments of $750 for 18 months. In addition to financial assistance,

participants received wraparound support. The pilot drew significant interest, receiving 2,400 applications. Pilot participants reflected the diversity of the applicant pool in race, ethnicity, age, and geographic distribution. A notable feature of the pilot was the unrestricted nature of the cash payments. Families had the complete freedom to use the funds as needed, addressing their unique and immediate financial requirements without any constraints.

This approach is well researched and acknowledges that each household is best positioned to determine what they need to achieve economic stability and mobility. The research presented today will focus on preliminary findings specifically from the Fairfax County pilot.

There is already mounting evidence, positive evidence, to support the efficacy and efficiency of basic income programs to reduce poverty, stimulate economic growth, promote entrepreneurship, and bring about social benefits. The target population for this program is identified as ALICE, Asset Limited, Income Restrained, Constrained, and Employed, a term defined by United Way. ALICE households earn more than the federal poverty level, but less than the necessary

income to cover their cost of living in our area. Many do not own a home, a car, or have enough savings to cover an unexpected expense of $400. These hard-working individuals, despite being employed, have difficulty making ends meet, which is exacerbated as the cost of essentials continues to rise faster than household incomes. When household income is suppressed by unemployment, underemployment, barriers to career advancement, and higher-paying jobs.

These systemic barriers block pathways to outward mobility for generations. Alice in Fairfax County is our neighbor, our friend, a family member, a colleague. Statistically, some of us in this room are Alice.

Alice are essential community members, teachers, administrative assistants, librarians, electricians, and they are the backbone of our economy. The Fairfax County Economic Mobility Pilot was funded through ARPA and Human Services Innovation Fund.

It's in direct alignment with the principles and goals of one Fairfax in the county strategic plan. In this pilot, we applied a comprehensive definition of upward mobility, which includes not only economic success, but also dignity, belonging, power, and autonomy.

We wanted to address the multifaceted nature of economic and social challenges and opportunities. The pilot was driven by a diverse cross-sector team that includes individuals with lived experience. Their insights and experience and expertise were crucial in designing and implementing a program that truly meets the needs of our community.

We also built the pilot on existing substructure of resources and partners so that we could integrate into other services and supports available in the county. This approach maximizes impact and creates a foundation to develop changes that can be sustainable long term.

And in meeting the moment of budget reductions, it's really essential now that we address the lack of pathways of opportunities in flexible public supports and policy and safety net gaps if we are to continue to thrive as a county.

This highlights the urgent need for systemic change to bridge the gap between wages and the cost of living, ensuring that hardworking families in Fairfax and across the region are not only able to survive, but thrive. Good afternoon. My name is Amy Best. I direct the Center for Social Science Research at George Mason. I'm here with Elise Storelli, my co-researcher. As researchers, our tasks have been to assess family and community impacts of the economic mobility pilot and inform county-led mobility strategies and systems change in order to reduce barriers to upward mobility for Alice families in the county.

We were not tasked with assessing the efficacy of the guaranteed income pilot, given the well-developed body of research that demonstrates clear, positive impacts of these policy initiatives. These unequal outcomes by race result from enduring systems of racial stratification and social enclosure, the persistence of racial discrimination in access to occupational sectors where wagers are higher, the racial income gap, historical and present-day barriers to equal educational opportunity, constrained opportunity for wealth accumulation caused by past and present residential segregation, all well documented by social science research, explain unequal economic outcomes by race. From wave one and wave two data collection,

we gained insight into how pilot participants use the funds to invest in their families and the short-term and early impacts of the pilot for them. Pilot participants were able to pay bills in full and on time and reduce debt, which minimized financial worry and allowed participants the mental space to plan for the future. As one participant shared, the money is oxygen for me. The outcome was being able to better budget, improve credit scores, and start to build modest savings for emergencies. Participants reported an increased sense of self-efficacy, that sense of being able

to achieve and accomplish tasks to have better control over their own lives, as well as improved well-being mentally and physically. Melissa was able to have much-needed dental procedure. She had postponed because of its cost. And Ben used the funds to sign his

family up for better health insurance so that they could get all the doctoring they can during the pilot period. Another clear standout among early impacts was participants' investments in their families. The majority reported being able to support their families financially and investing in their children and their children's futures. This was expressed in ways both big and small.

For some families, it meant a first-time Christmas tree or kids' coloring books. For others, it meant swim lessons and rec soccer, activities that contribute to healthy social and emotional development for kids. Or it might have been a family camping trip. Larissa, as we introduced earlier invested in her teenage son by allowing him to not work in order to help pay their rent and instead join a boxing gym, which for Larissa was a big relief since at the pilot's midpoint, he had cut out soda and importantly quit vaping. Pilot participants reported being more involved

and more connected to their community, which translated into a stronger sense of belonging. Several reported pride in being able to give back. Zania, who is a full-time Fairfax County public school teacher, was able to participate for the first time in a fundraising event for her child's school. Others reported participating more fully in community and neighborhood events, feeling valued for their contribution of their time and commitment to community betterment, which for Melissa involved helping to organize several outdoor outings with local teens.

Overall, our mid-pilot data shows transformational effects. That's meant greater financial stabilization for all pilot participants. When participants used funds for debt reduction and modest savings, this allowed them to better weather financial shocks. They could better absorb unanticipated expenses, like Xenia, who had to pay more car insurance for her daughter, a newly licensed driver, when she began commuting to college. Other participants weathered rent increases, needed car repairs, and additional child care costs that came with a new and better

job. Pilot funds also enabled families to make mobility investments. That meant using funds to gain credentials and accelerating their educational pathway. Michelle was able to double up on her coursework toward her teaching credential, and Azum completed several tech certificates to strengthen his IT credentials, just like ISU. At Wave 2 data collection, we saw indications of increased connection to county resources and opportunities, like more active involvement in the Financial Empowerment Center, including their financial workshops and new home buyer classes,

which suggests the pilot has been an important connector to other valuable support networks and resources. These mobility investments extend to children as well. At seven months into the pilot, Z had made plans to open a 529 college savings account for his two kids. Others gained new freedoms because of the pilot funds. Not having to continue with a second job on top of full-time work, allowed for more sleep, or more time to spend with their children at the pool or the park.

When Z was able to cut hours from his second job due to the pilot funds, he spent time watching over his kids and other neighborhood kids as they played outside, which freed up other neighborhood parents to run needed errands. He was able to be present for his family and his community, which brought a sense of joy, connection, and fulfillment, which is its own kind of prosperity.

Despite these positive transformations, and there are many, midpoint data also showed pilot participants face persistent barriers, some more profound than others. 82% of Wave 1 survey respondents reported wages inadequate to cover basic needs, either most of the time or some of the time.

By Wave 2, the number who reported insufficient wages to cover basic needs remained little changed. Among immigrant families, prior career credentials aren't consistently recognized post-migration, producing workforce gaps, and stalled career advancement.

The high cost of child care remains a major challenge, not only in terms of actual cost, but the deferred wages from second-parent earners who forego work to care for children not yet school age. For households with one parent, child care cost burden is acutely felt.

Among all families, the high cost of housing was a continued barrier for mobility. Even at wave two, the pilot's midpoint, paying rent was the second most common way that funds were spent. These system level barriers have differential and uneven effects based on the intersection of race and gender, as well as age, immigrant status, and occupation, as well as where you live.

During the final wave of data collection taking place now, we will continue to examine barriers to upward mobility, families confront, as well as the more lasting gains from the pilot now that it has ended, in the hopes that this research can inform promising, innovative cross-system approaches.
